description: Team Atlas: six students from Birzeit University, Palestine, taking on Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data. We want to help smallholder farmers adapt what and when they plant as the climate changes, using NASA data like IMERG rainfall and SMAP soil moisture. Our skills: Python, data analysis, AI, research and visual design. We're looking for teammates strong in geospatial data (GIS, remote sensing), web or mobile development, or agriculture. Join us to build something real for farmers.
summary: Ardi lets a rainfed farmer compare their current crop rotation with two alternatives, in an average season and in the 5th-driest of 27 seasons in NASA's satellite rain record for their area. It turns NASA GPM IMERG rain and NASA POWER heat records into four transparent scores, shows MODIS and SRTM as context, and ends with a plain-Arabic farmer card that can be read aloud, as a guide, not a rule.
details:
Problem. Rainfed farmers on the Jenin plain choose next season's crops under unreliable rain. A rotation that works in an average year can fail in a dry one, and growing the same cereal year after year builds up pests and disease and drains the soil. In Jenin Governorate, 73,973 of 77,183 dunums of field crops (about 96%) were rainfed in 2020/21, and wheat covered 39% (PCBS & Ministry of Agriculture, Agricultural Census 2021). Jenin is our pilot example; the NASA layer works for any rainfed region. Our pilot point is an open field-crop strip on the Arraba–Burqin plain (32.43° N, 35.22° E). Its rainfed status has not been confirmed on the ground.

How it works. The farmer picks their current rotation (A). Ardi reads two files: NASA indicators for the area around the point, and a local crop pack. It flags any rotation that puts the same crop family in two consecutive years. It scores each rotation from 0 to 100 on four things:

- water: the share of past seasons with at least each crop's minimum rain (FAO ECOCROP), from IMERG;

- stage risk: the share of seasons without a heat or dry-spell hit at the sensitive stage. A hit is 5 or more days above 32 °C in March–May (POWER), or 3 or more dry spells of 10+ days in January–March (IMERG). These cut-offs are our choice, not published values;

- soil: bare months and a legume credit, from the crop pack;

- income: yield × price, discounted by the water score, using 2021 average producer prices for wheat and barley (PCBS) and our own assumptions for lentil and bitter vetch.

The farmer's priority (save water, soil first, income, balanced) sets the weights. Separately, each rotation gets a pass/fail line for the 5th-driest of 27 October–May seasons (2007/08, 363 mm). The output is three cards (A = current, B = wheat ↔ lentil, C = barley ↔ bitter vetch). Each card shows why it was suggested, the evidence, benefits, gaps and what a local expert should check, and the app ends with an Arabic farmer card with an English line. A Listen button reads the card aloud in Arabic using the device's own text-to-speech, for farmers who prefer listening to reading.

The farmer's own knowledge. Satellites describe the area, not the inside of one plot: SRTM heights around our point differ by only 5 m across 480 m, which is within its error. So Ardi asks the farmer what differs inside the plot (a low spot where water collects, a high or stony edge, a sloping part, edges weaker than the middle) and adds one plain note for each, labelled "from you" and "check locally". These notes do not change the scores.

What the real data shows. With the balanced priority, barley ↔ bitter vetch scores 71 of 100 and holds up in the 2007/08 dry season. Wheat ↔ lentil is close behind at 66, and wheat every year scores 52 and breaks the crop-family rule. Both rotations with wheat fail the dry season in the wheat year, because wheat's minimum is about 400 mm and that season had 363 mm. That gap is small and within satellite-rain error, so we show it as a warning, not a verdict: wheat's minimum was missed in 6 of 27 seasons, barley's and lentil's in none. The order of the options is the same under all four priorities; only the scores change. Rain did not change between the two halves of the record (474 vs 473 mm), but heat days above 32 °C in March–May rose from 2.8 to 4.6 a season.

Benefits. Farmers see a rotation's trade-offs in the kind of dry season their area has actually had, explained in Arabic, with every number labelled by its dataset, resolution and years. Ardi is designed to add NASA historical records, a Palestinian rainfed crop pack and evidence labels to rotation planning that tools like ROTOR and DSSAT already research.

What we hope to achieve. Test the cards with farmers in Jenin and validate the crop rules with local agronomists. Add local soil data (a soil test or soil map) and satellite soil moisture, which are not in this version. Add crop packs for other rainfed regions; the NASA layer stays the same and only the local pack changes. Make the start easier: find the land by phone GPS or by tapping the map, add Arabic voice read-out, and add offline use for low connectivity.

Limits. Satellite and grid data describe the area, not the plot. Rotation A, the farmer "Abu Ahmad" and all crop values are illustrative until a farmer or agronomist confirms them. The dry season is a stress test from history, not a forecast. No soil test or soil-moisture data is used yet; the soil score is a rule (legume share and sowing-calendar bare months), not a soil measurement. The rain minimums are FAO ECOCROP lower limits, not harvest thresholds, and the heat and dry-spell cut-offs are our choice. Our vegetation check is weak: in only 2 of the 5 driest seasons was the MODIS greenness peak below normal (Spearman ρ = −0.11, 25 seasons), and we report it as weak. The read-aloud voice is machine speech and has not been tested with farmers. Ardi supports the farmer's judgment; it never replaces it.

Tools and languages. HTML, CSS and JavaScript (a static page on GitHub Pages); Python (requests, pandas, numpy) for data extraction; NASA POWER API, NASA AppEEARS, NASA Giovanni / GES DISC; Playwright and ffmpeg for screen recordings; Claude Slides for the 7-slide deck; d3-geo and Natural Earth land data for the globe on slide 1; a QR code generated by a Python library for the demo slide.
